questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of an Integral
questions.problem:
Given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={t}^{3}.$ Thus, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{{\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Inverse Laplace Transform Using the Integral Rule
questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{6}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{6}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{4!}{{s}^{4+1}}} \\  & ={t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{4}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+4)},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ $0$, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-5}}\,\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of an Integral
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\mathcal{L}\{\cos(\omega t)\}  = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ for $s>0,$  find the Laplace transform of

$$
\displaystyle g(t)= \int_{0}^{t} \cos\big(\pi\tau\big) \, \textrm{d}\tau, \quad s>0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau) \, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t) = \cos(\pi t).$ Thus, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s) = \dfrac{1}{s(s-1)}, \qquad s > 1
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}=\dfrac{1}{s-a},\ s>a.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s) = \frac{1}{s(s-1)} = \frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s) = \dfrac{1}{s-1}.$
Also, we know that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={e}^{τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}A(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
= \dfrac{1}{s}\int_0^{\infty}{ e^{-st} A'(t)} \,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Finally, using that $A'(t) = f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
